name: Saint Francis, the Franciscan order, and its ironic institutional fate
plain_explanation: Saint Francis of Assisi renounced wealth after a sudden act of compassion toward a leper, founding an order of followers vowed to complete, radical poverty (begging their bread, refusing even houses or churches). Innocent III shrewdly recognized the order in 1209/1210, keeping it within orthodoxy rather than letting it become another heretical 'Poor Men of Lyons.' But within a generation of Francis's death, his own order abandoned poverty (his successor Brother Elias 'wallowed in luxury'), became a recruiting arm for factional wars, staffed much of the Inquisition, and condemned as heretical (in 1323) the 'Spirituals' who tried to remain faithful to Francis's original ideal.
precise_definition: The mendicant religious order founded by Saint Francis of Assisi (recognized by Innocent III, 1209/1210), originally committed to absolute poverty and itinerant preaching, whose subsequent institutional history (wealth, involvement in the Inquisition, persecution of its own 'Spiritual' faction) Russell presents as a bitterly ironic betrayal of its founder's aims.
why_it_mattered: It illustrates, for Russell, a recurring historical pattern in which a genuinely selfless religious impulse is captured and redirected by institutional and political interests -- and it sets up the later chapter on Franciscan schoolmen (Roger Bacon, Duns Scotus, Occam), the order that, ironically, produced the most independent-minded philosophers of the following century.
historical_origin: Founded by Saint Francis of Assisi (1181/1182-1226) following his renunciation of his family's wealth; formally recognized by Innocent III in 1209 or 1210.
examples: Francis's hymn to the sun, written shortly before his death, which Russell compares to the sun-worship of Akhnaton while noting it remains distinctly Christian
Francis's 1219 journey to preach before the Muslim sultan, who received him courteously but did not convert
Francis's distress on returning to find his followers had built themselves a permanent house, contrary to his ideal of total poverty
competing_positions: Saint Dominic's order, which prioritized learning and doctrinal combat over Francis's radical poverty ideal from the start
influence_on_later_thinkers: The later Franciscan intellectual tradition (Roger Bacon, Duns Scotus, William of Occam), despite Francis's own personal dislike of learning, becomes the source of the most philosophically original scholastics of the following century, as the next chapter notes.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Franciscans became chief conductors of the Inquisition in several countries and recruiting agents in the wars of Guelfs and Ghibellines -- outcomes Russell judges to be the 'most bitterly ironical' possible given Francis's own character and aims.
